glossary.title: Why the Oil Crisis Is (Secretly) Good...
glossary.llm_summary: Strait of Hormuz oil crisis framed as asymmetric US advantage. US is world's largest oil producer and LNG exporter — benefits from supply tightness. Asia (China, India, Japan, South Korea) takes 75% of Persian Gulf oil and faces supply disruption risk. Geopolitical angle: Hormuz disruption as US leverage in US-China trade negotiations. Indirectly bullish for gold via USD strength and geopolitical uncertainty, but no direct gold analysis.
glossary.transcript_text: Right now, the world thinks it's watching an oil crisis unfold. And on the surface, it makes sense why. Because energy markets are all over the place, and governments across Europe and Asia are scrambling to hold emergency meetings. And all of the panic can be traced back to one place, the straight of Hormuz, a narrow strip of water that provides the only sea passage from the Persian Gulf to the open ocean. And every single day, roughly 20% of the world's oil passes through it, which makes it the single most important choke point on the planet. And the general consensus is pretty clear. If something goes wrong here, the global economy is totally But maybe that's just the story we're being told. And maybe it's only half the story, because the truth is there's a lot more going on here. Because the real story isn't just about what's happening. It's about who it's happening to. Because oil shocks don't hit the world equally, and they never have. Because while some economies get crushed, others quietly benefit. And that's what this story is really about. It's not a story about a crisis. It's about positioning. Because most people still think this plays out like it did 20 years ago where instability in the Middle East leads to an oil shock which eventually hits the US economy. And for a long time, this was true because 20 years ago, the United States was heavily dependent on foreign oil. In fact, roughly 60% of the total petroleum consumption was from imports. So when the global supply got disrupted, the impact was immediate. Prices spiked, inflation surged, and the economy hit pause. It was a clear linear relationship. But that version of the world doesn't exist anymore. Because over the past two decades, something changed. New drilling techniques unlocked massive shale reserves for the United States. And production boomed. And suddenly, the United States didn't just reduce its dependence on foreign oil, it flipped the entire script. Because if you fast forward to the present, the United States is the largest oil producer in the world. Which means the old narrative, it's outdated because now the United States isn't on the same side of the trade anymore. So now the question becomes then who actually is exposed? And this is where you get to the real story because most of the oil moving through the straight of Hormuz isn't going to the United States. In fact, only 2 and 12% of it is. The majority of the oil in the Middle East is going somewhere else to Asia and more specifically China, India, Japan, and South Korea. Because together, these four countries account for roughly 75% of all the oil moving through the straight. So when people say a disruption here will shock the global economy, they're not wrong. But they're also missing something very important. It's an asymmetric shock. And it doesn't hit everyone equally. Because for the United States, a disruption mostly just becomes a price problem. And that's because oil is globally priced. So if supply tightens anywhere, oil prices rise all over, which hurts. But it's at least manageable. But for Asia, it's different because it isn't just a price problem. It also becomes a supply problem. And those are very different things because higher prices slow you down. But losing access to your energy supply, well, that's when things can start to break. Where factories slow, energy gets rationed, and production stalls. It's the same event, but with completely different consequences. And this is where the story shifts from crisis to positioning because when supply tightens and prices rise, it creates winners and losers. And right now, the United States is on the winning side because higher prices don't just hurt. It also generates revenue for producers, for exporters, and for energy companies. And the United States just happens to be the world's largest oil producer, which means the same shock that's creating global pain is also stimulating parts of the US economy. But oil is also only half the story because there's a second layer that most people are completely overlooking. Natural gas. Because the Middle East is also one of the largest exporters of liqufied natural gas in the world. And just like oil, a massive portion of it flows through the straight of Hormuz. In fact, it's roughly 20% of the global supply of liqufied natural gas. And countries like Qatar and the United Arab Emirates send over 90% of their liqufied natural gas exports through the strait. So if the straight gets disrupted, it's not just the oil markets that tighten, it's gas markets, too. And once again, this is where the United States shows up. Because over the past decade, the United States has quietly become the largest exporter of liqufied natural gas in the world, which means the same dynamic repeats. One region loses supply and another steps in to sell it. And the markets are already beginning to react to this, which is why we're seeing energy companies rise and exporters benefit. Venture Global, one of the fastest growing LNG exporters, has seen its stock jump nearly 40% in the past month. And Chener Energy, the largest LNG exporter in the US, is up nearly 15%. And on the crude oil side, we're seeing the same thing. And that's because scarcity doesn't just create risk, it creates opportunity. They've been actively diversifying suppliers, building strategic reserves, and expanding imports from other countries like Russia, Brazil, and Venezuela. But even though China has hedged themselves with safeguards to buy them time, they still haven't fully eliminated the risk, and they're still exposed. Because China is the largest importer of oil in the world. They consume around 15 to 16 million barrels per day, and roughly 11 million of those barrels are imported. And a huge portion of that comes from one region, the Middle East, flowing directly through the Straight of Hormuz, which means the safeguards they've built don't eliminate the risk. They just delay it. Because in the short term, China can probably absorb the shock. In the medium-term, they start having to draw down on their reserves. But if the disruption lasts long enough, well, that's when the real problems begin, where it goes from an inconvenience to a structural problem. And that's because China doesn't just use energy, it runs on it. From manufacturing to exports to their industrial output, the core of China's economy depends on a constant flow of energy. And when that flow gets disrupted, then the pressure builds. Which brings us to the part of the story that almost nobody seems to be talking about. And the main takeaway for this whole thing, because if you zoom out for a second, something about this entire situation looks strange. Not the conflict itself, because conflicts happen all the time, especially in the Middle East, but the timing of it. Because right as tensions around the straight of Hormuz started escalating, something else was happening. Trade negotiations between the United States and China were reaching a critical point. Whether it was tariffs, technology restrictions, or supply chain decoupling, for years, the economic and political relationship between the world's two largest economies has slowly been unraveling. And maybe that's where the truth in this conflict really is. Because maybe negotiations are not just about finding a solution. Maybe they're about leverage. And if that's true, well, leverage comes from pressure. Economic pressure, market pressure, and sometimes energy pressure. And when you start looking at the whole situation through that lens, the straight of Hormuz stops looking like an energy story and starts looking like it may be a geopolitical story between China and the United States. Because if one country can tolerate the shock while another country feels the structural pressure from it, then the shock itself becomes leverage. Which means maybe the straight of Hormuz isn't just a choke point for oil and maybe it's also a choke point for power. [music]

glossary.title: How Capital Cycles Create 100 Baggers In Plain Sight
glossary.llm_summary: Django Davidson interview on capital cycle investing framework applied to mining. Framework origin: Jeremy Grantham/GMO 1990s — supply is measurable, demand is storytelling; focus on supply constraints. Codified in Edward Chancellor's book 'Capital Account' (out of print, ~$2,000 on eBay). Core principle: long-run share price is driven by return on capital, not earnings. Industries with declining returns on capital (hyperscalers spending $700B on data centers, OpenAI offering 17.5% guaranteed returns to PE) will disappoint. Industries with rising returns (constrained supply, no new capacity being built) will compound. Incentives drive booms: promoters raise $1 → market values at $3-10 → fee networks of banks, intermediaries sustain momentum. Capital cycle as contrarian guard rails: avoid mass capacity addition + IPO boom (correctly warned on lithium). Look for bust-phase industries where no new supply being built. Rick Rule quoted: 'if you're not a contrarian you're going to be a victim.' Applied to ASX mining: lithium avoided on supply glut; beaten-down mining sectors with rising returns on capital now at sweet spot of capital cycle. The key behavioral edge: as prices rise, investor returns on capital definitionally fall — yet animal spirits make investors more enthusiastic at exactly the wrong time.

glossary.llm_summary: Mechanistic explanation for why gold falls during geopolitical crises before rallying sharply. Oil spike → inflation expectations rise → Fed cannot cut rates → bond yields rise (US 10y competing at ~5%) → dollar strengthens → three simultaneous headwinds crush gold. Historical pattern validated across every major oil shock: 1973 OPEC embargo (gold +150% over 2 years, +2300% 1971-1980 full period); 1979 Iranian Revolution (+89% next 12 months); 1991 Gulf War (+10% pop); post-9/11 ($250→$1,900 decade bull run); 2022 Ukraine (broke $2,000). Four-phase recovery: Phase 1 (week 1-4 panic); Phase 2 (month 2-3 gold drops 15-20%, retail capitulates — worst time to sell); Phase 3 (month 4-18, structural bid returns, miners lever up); Phase 4 (month 12+, new all-time highs). Current setup more extreme than any prior oil shock: $38T US debt, 1,000+ tons/yr central bank buying, three-year silver supply deficit, institutional smart money at extreme short — historically precedes large rallies. Five sector outperformers during crises: gold miners (GDX, 2-3x leverage to gold), silver (SLV), energy (XLE, Strait of Hormuz = 20% of world oil), defense (ITA, +47% vs S&P post-9/11), utilities (XLU, flat in 2022 when S&P -15%).

glossary.llm_summary: US military posture in the Iran war is shifting from air power to ground-option readiness. Two Marine Expeditionary Units (~4,400 troops) deployed to the Persian Gulf. Escalation spectrum analyzed: special forces raids on nuclear stockpile (Isfahan/Fordow) or missile factories; limited territorial seizures of Strait of Hormuz islands (Kish, Qeshm, Abu Musa, Greater/Lesser Tumb) and Kharg Island oil infrastructure; full-scale invasion requiring 200,000+ troops assessed as strategic disaster comparable to Iraq but harder. Key asymmetry: Iran only needs to survive each day while US needs decisive victory. IRGC is decentralized (31 autonomous brigades), so leadership decapitation has limited effect. Amphibious assault on defended coastline last attempted in Korea 1950. Bottom line: ground operations remain possible but each step escalates political and military costs exponentially; rivals (Russia, China) exploit US distraction in other theaters.

The last time America attempted a truly contested landing against a defended coastline was during the Korean War in 1950. Doing so today would expose landing forces to drones, anti-ship missiles, coastal defenses, and artillery. Even if the initial assault succeeded, American troops could quickly find themselves fighting in dense urban areas where many of their technological advantages begin to fade. Moreover, the geography and distance of such an operation favor. Iranian forces would be operating close to their own bases, supply lines, and missile systems, while American troops would depend on ships and regional bases that could themselves become targets. For that reason, focusing on Iran's isolated islands is a far more manageable objective than the large coastal cities. Yet, perhaps the hardest question of all is what happens after. Capturing territory is one thing. holding it and eventually getting out is something else entirely. The final option, and the most dramatic one, would be a full-scale invasion, one aimed either at dismantling Iran's conventional military forces or bringing down the Islamic Republic altogether. But an operation of this scale would come at an enormous cost. For comparison, the invasion of Iraq in 2003 required more than 6 months to assemble around 200,000 soldiers in the region. Iran, however, is larger in size and population and is more mountainous. So, the required number of troops and resources would be many times that of the Iraqi experience. The United States would also need regional support. Neighboring countries would have to host American troops and allow supply lines to run through their territory. Yet few governments appear to have an appetite for total war. Then there is the political challenge at home. A war of this scale would require massive funding and long-term commitment. Under US law, Congress would almost certainly need to approve such an operation. Without broad public support, sustaining a prolonged ground war would be extremely difficult. Fortunately, we're not there yet. A full-scale invasion is unlikely. Only a major economic or military blow from Iran would be enough to push public opinion toward a ground war. Assuming that obstacles such as funding, mobilization, popular support, and regional logistics were overcome, Washington could then begin assembling the forces required for a fullscale invasion. This would likely involve a buildup of hundreds of thousands of troops with the initial phase focusing on amphibious landings along Iran's southern coast and a push toward major cities and the oilrich province of Kuzan. American forces could then attempt to weaken the Iranian military while supporting local opposition groups, similar to the strategy used in Afghanistan in 2001. or they might attempt a direct advance toward Thran as they did with Baghdad 2 years later. Either way, a full-scale invasion of Iran would be nothing short of a strategic disaster. There would be no quick victory. It would likely unfold over months or years, especially if the United States relied on proxy forces rather than committing to a direct advance into the Iranian interior. And even then, victory on the battlefield would only mark the beginning of a far longer phase. Iran's population is large, its terrain is difficult, and stabilizing the country could tie down American forces for years, if not decades. All it would do is drain American resources away from Europe and Asia. And when a superpower is busy in one theater, its rivals rehearse in another. I've been your host Shervan from Caspian Report. glossary.title: Forget FalconBridge. NexGen is Gilman's Big Score
glossary.llm_summary: Warren Gilman career story focused on his Hong Kong years and NexGen Energy's Arrow uranium deposit. Key narrative: moved to Hong Kong 1999 (escaped Perth during gold's $200 bottom) → became the only mining expert working with Lee Ka-shing during China's commodity supercycle emergence → worked on landmark deals including MinMetals/Falconbridge, Placer+Barrick merger, Meridian Gold IPO. In Hong Kong in 2005-2007: China's MinMetals, Jinchuan, Zin were leading international mining M&A. Pattern recognized: large, world-class ore bodies almost inevitably end up in major integrated miners' portfolios. NexGen's Arrow deposit (Athabasca Basin) just received final permits after 10 years — Lee Ka-shing cornerstone investor via $60M convertible arranged by cold call 10 years ago. Iran war as direct uranium demand catalyst: parallels 1973 Arab oil embargo which sparked a decade of nuclear buildout for energy security. BHP/Rio historically reluctant on uranium despite Olympic Dam, but oil companies (BP once owned copper/gold/lime mines via Selection Trust acquisition) may return to mining for nuclear feedstock. Energy security imperative now more acute than any time since 1973.

glossary.title: What Gold’s Past Tells Us About Its Future
glossary.llm_summary: Interview with Sean (Australian gold corporate historian) on the current gold mining bull market. Sean started in the industry in 1984 — in the shadow of the 1980 $850 gold peak. Key historical pattern: gold stocks lagged the 1980 gold price spike (investors were too panicked to buy equities), then boomed in 1986-87 on relative multiple expansion — not DCF justification, just EV-per-resource-ounce comparisons. Analogy: similar to dot-com era where earnings multiples were meaningless but relative multiples still drove markets. Current bull market: gold stocks hottest in years, but generalists not yet in. Institutional threshold effect: when stocks cross $1B market cap, pension funds can invest regardless of insider valuation concerns — once this happens, momentum accelerates and insiders feel valuations are 'nuts' but stocks keep going. Narrative follows price (Michael Cheney: 'none of the people telling you where it's going predicted the boom'). Charts and ratios (gold stocks vs gold price, gold vs S&P) more useful than fundamentals for timing cyclical tops. Capital must flow somewhere — gold is a natural destination when money supply expands. New Zealand gold region (Enduro-associated consolidation play) highlighted as exciting. Strong view: current setup could develop into one of the greatest gold equity bull markets in history if generalist capital finally rotates in.

glossary.title: Why Aluminium Just Went Vertical
glossary.llm_summary: Deep dive into aluminium supply chain dynamics. Rule of thumb: 5 tons bauxite → 2 tons alumina → 1 ton primary aluminium. 2024-2025 alumina price spike caused by converging shocks: Quinana refinery shutdown (Queensland), Rio Tinto force majeure on Queensland gas supply, Brazilian refinery disruption, Guinea bauxite disruptions (world's largest non-China bauxite source). China Yunnan hydro power adequate in 2025, preventing smelting cuts. Result: alumina price spike then collapse — now ~40% of global alumina refining sector loss-making (below cost curve). Primary aluminium price performing well due to: China 45M ton smelting capacity cap (no new capacity), strong demand (EVs, construction), tariff speculation on US imports. Debate on integrated vs non-integrated model (Rio Tinto): historically vertically integrated gave stability through cycle, but spot bauxite/alumina markets now viable. ASX relevance: Rio Tinto's aluminium division (bauxite in QLD, alumina at Yarwun/QAL, smelting at Tomago/Portland) directly affected. Aluminium demand slow-burn growth — world needs at least one new smelter per year indefinitely.

glossary.llm_summary: Leon from Arrakis Global — generalist macro fund manager — discusses investment philosophy and commodity themes. Core philosophy: don't lose money, cut positions at 2% drawdown, maximum cognitive flexibility across asset classes. Process evolution from fundamental to incorporating momentum, market structure, narrative + price action as fluid interacting system. Key current themes: European defense (paradigm shift confirmed by Trump-Vance Munich Security Conference + Zelensky White House moment — thesis: JD Vance lecturing European leaders = fundamental NATO commitment shift); commodities via 'rolling crackup' supply constraint thesis. Each commodity hits its shortage wall independently (TTF gas 2021, LME nickel 2022, oil Ukraine 2022, uranium 2023, copper 2024 fits/starts). Now seeing rare convergence where all commodities moving together on the same days — possibly Rolling Crackup thesis merging with India emerging demand + dollar debasement narrative. AI data center boom exhibits classic bubble misallocation signals: OpenAI offering guaranteed 17.5% returns to PE, massive fee networks sustaining momentum. Contrasts with commodity markets where forcing function (someone needs delivery tomorrow, price-inelastic) rewards active research over passive allocation.

glossary.title: Why Smart Money Is Buying Energy Chaos (Saul Kavonic)
glossary.llm_summary: Deep interview with energy analyst Saul Kavonic on Australian oil and gas investment. Thesis: go long 'energy policy chaos' — Australian policymakers' track record of incompetence creates structural upside for domestic gas producers and electricity generators with gas exposure. Current oil/gas equities pricing in $60-62/bbl long-term oil — structurally low, since US shale supply declines below $55 WTI. Three layers of Australian energy market: macro oil (geopolitical, Iran war → oil $70→$90+); macro LNG (global, still young market); domestic gas (parochial, policy-driven, east coast reservation policies). Background: 2007-2014 boom followed by 2014-2020 bust (ESG pressure + COVID oversupply). ESG headwinds now fading, funding returning. Iran war: every $10 oil rise costs import-dependent countries $4-5B/yr extra. glossary.title: The New Commodity Supercycle Is Already Here (Paulo Macro)
glossary.llm_summary: Paulo Macro presents thesis that the commodity supercycle is underway but structurally different from the 2000s China demand-pull boom. In 2000s: $300B AUM flooded commodities on China demand — topped 2011, then 10+ years underinvestment. Current cycle: supply-constrained, not demand-pulled. Rolling crackups: individual commodities hit shortage walls sequentially rather than all rising together — European TTF gas (fall 2021), LME nickel $80,000/t (Feb 2022, trades busted), oil $120 on Ukraine invasion, uranium $100+ (2023), copper (2024 fits/starts). Key insight: 'forcing function' in commodities (someone needs delivery tomorrow, price-inelastic) rewards active research unlike fixed income (Fed-watching) and equities (passive/buybacks = momentum). Dollar has strengthened 10 years (suppressing EM demand) but Trump debasement narrative now kicking — India GDP per capita hitting S-curve for commodity-intensive growth. Signs emerging that all commodities moving together again like 2000s (energy + metals + uranium + gold correlating) — possible convergence of Rolling Crackup + India demand + debasement. Capital cycle guard rails: warned on lithium (correctly) — mass capacity addition + IPO boom = supply glut. Platinum: up 60% in 3 months after 12 months flat (patience rewarded). Contrarian + capital cycle discipline = less bad decisions.
glossary.transcript_text: My bigger takeaway was how unsynchronized the global economy seems to be now in terms of where we are in the cycle. Usually it's you know US catches a cold the rest of the world gets the flu maybe with a lag. I don't know if that's true this time because Hong Kong and China seem to be in flecting off the lows. Hello Macro. Thank you so much for for joining us again mate. It's been a while since we last spoke and there has been heaps happening in the world of of metals and mining and markets more broadly. One of the one of the big themes that I'm keen to jump into first is your idea of the the present super cycle we're in and how that kind of contrasts with the China bull market that we saw in the 2000s where you really sort of cut your teeth in. So, I'd love to kind of start right there and and hear your your evolution on thinking in this this super cycle, the the rolling crackups thesis that you have and and everything related. >> Oh, wow. Um, well, first off, thanks fellas for uh having me back. Um, I guess it's I can't believe a year has gone by if I think it's been a year. And uh I um I I I'm sorry. I know you guys have been reaching out for uh for a while now to um to have me back and it's uh I've just been completely snowed. uh as I think you boys like to say, although it never snows in Australia, so I don't know why you guys say it, but uh um you're taking me way back. Uh this is kind of one of my first framework notes when I first moved to Substack. So it's um it's like really big picture how I think about the world in comparing today or more like comparing and contrasting today versus the 2000s. Um so happy to jump in right there. I think for me in starting out in the 2000s especially with a commodity bent um as a kind of a young bloke starting in the business and actually uh one of my first assignments was Australian equities. So I've got a very soft sweet spot in my heart for uh you boys down under um and been there many times and uh in my 20s starting out the cycle was just getting going. But there were a couple of key points that were different then versus today. Um for one you had a very clear demand pull uh from the emerging China. We all know that story. But uh that kind of measure of a rise a rising tide lifting all boats uh did some interesting things to a space that had been mostly cast aside for you know the better part of uh 20 plus years. Um going back all the way to the 70s which was kind of our last big commodity secular bull. Um, in this case with China's coming out party after the WTO and the rise of China uh and Chinese demand hitting that kind of scurve of GDP per capita that a lot of people talk about when they think about global south, India and Southeast Asia today. You had a situation where two things happened at once. You had that kind of general demand pull where the entire demand curve pushes out and to the right. And you also had an interesting exercise come out, I believe around 2004, where McKenzie dropped a a a research note uh report uh arguing that if you took your typical equity and bond uh fixed uh uh fixed income allocation uh and added a passive commodity exposure via futures to those two uh even around the edges. Uh what they found was two amazing things. one, the returns from commodities historically were uncorrelated uh near zero to either of those asset classes. So it made sense as a bolt-on to 60/40 and more importantly that as all of these curves which naturally want to sit in contango, if you want to store a commodity, you need a contango where the near-term price is cheaper to the fartherdated price to pay for shipping, storage, in particular storage and insurance. Then as you backwardate, which is the curve's way of punishing stores and calling supplies out to the market, you passively begin to collect a yield. So you were basically ringing the dinner bell for pension fund allocators who were looking for other options. And remember this is in the early mid 2000s when hedge funds and alternatives were just starting to get going. So, you know, hedge funds were in an allocatable asset class the way private equity and credit is today among universities where 40% of their their billion-dollar endowments are in in privates. Back then, it was really stocks and bonds and a little around the edges and the David Swinson Yale University CIOS of the world were playing with alternatives uh around the edges, but the mass market kind of longdated saver, insurance companies, pensions, what have you, were only starting to wake up to this. This McKenzie report woke people up to the fact that you had non-correlated A and positive ruled yield B. And if you basically tell somebody that you have an uncorrelated asset class that generates a positive yield in an environment like the early mid200s when the Fed had cut to 1% and basically kicked off the real estate bubble in the US. That was like ringing the dinner bell for large allocators. And so commodities rose as an asset class and we saw $300 billion of AUM flood into the space during that boom in the 2000s which all of course uh was you know miraculously crowned and ended with the demise of Lehman Brothers and the financial crisis in08. There was a an echo boom coming out of that but by 2011 that was the ultimate top of commodities and emerging markets and we were done. The difference this time uh kind of setting the table with that is you don't have a very clear uh demand pull in one particular place per se. Uh the dollar has been gradually strengthening for 10 years which has kind of been a boot on the neck of EM since 2011 as we know. Um more recently Trump seems to want to change that. The debasement trade is underway. It's starting to catch fire as a longer term narrative. Weaker dollar will you know be a kick in the butt for emerging market demand. uh that's all great and maybe India owns the second half of the 2020s or the 2030s uh and some of these economies very large are hitting their S- curves now you know as they kick through 2500 $3,000 GDP per capita but the real driver so far of commodities has been the supply constraint that followed the boom uh where basically the tide went out for 10 plus years uh uh via underinvestment and that underinvestment shifts the supply curve in as opposed to the China story which pushed the demand curve out. The outcome is the same. You get a general appreciation starting in the price level, but it reflects in the market in a different way. Whereas the backward dating curves driven by China is a rising tide that lifts pretty much all commodity boats at around the same time. Here what we're seeing is different commodities run into the wall of shortage or you know a production crack up or a slip up at different points in time which actually is Christmas for an active commodity manager or someone who uh wants to take a longer short you know active approach and I I call this also the forcing function in commodities they seem to do nothing for a long time and then suddenly they'll work 50% out of nowhere over a few weeks or months and that forcing function in commodities is expressed because someone has a problem somewhere or needs delivery tomorrow. Uh they're price insensitive and they need to pay that price. It's the opposite effect of what's happening in fixed income and equities where the forcing function for fixed income for example you know nobody does fundamental work on rates anymore. I mean they do but they're wasting their time. you talk to a rates guy or a credit guy um who used to do this 20 years ago, he'll tell you he used to build fundamental models around rates, you know, growth, inflation, what have you. Today, he spends almost all of his time wondering what's the Fed going to do? What's the Treasury going to do with the TGA, the RP at the Fed, the interplay of liquidity up, liquidity down, what does that do to bond prices, the the changing mix in coupons versus T bills, how that changes bond prices. It's all flow. In equities, you guys are well aware of the drive of passive, the buybacks that chew through the float. And the more that you can quickly buy back stock, the more that momentum kicks in puts you into mega cap territory. Uh the inelasticity as these companies get bigger. glossary.title: How the Iran War will actually end
glossary.llm_summary: Iran war is being determined by three pressure points: munitions, markets, and midterms. The US burned through ~800 Patriot interceptors in the first 5 days and is cannibalising missile systems from Asia-Pacific to sustain the campaign. Production of SM-3 and PAC-3 interceptors is measured in dozens per year — one night of missile defence can erase months of output. On the market side, Strait of Hormuz closure is rippling through freight, fertiliser, food prices, and tech data centres (Iran has targeted Amazon AWS infrastructure in UAE and Bahrain). The Magnificent 7 tech companies — 60% of S&P 500 returns in 2023 — are now legitimate IRGC targets. Politically, the 2026 US midterms create a hard ceiling on Trump's war duration. Iran's strategy is to stretch missile supply chains, unsettle markets, and wait for political pressure to build in Washington. The war ends when all three pressure points converge simultaneously.
glossary.transcript_text: People often imagine armed conflicts being won or lost on the battlefield. Armies advance, enemies retreat, and eventually one side wins. But modern wars rarely end that way. They end when three things start breaking at the same time. Munitions, markets, and midterms. These pressure points determine how long hostilities can realistically continue. In the first 5 days of this war, the United States burned through roughly 800 Patriot interceptors. Once munitions begin to run low, commanders must face difficult choices. They can either slow the pace of operations or redeploy assets from elsewhere. The Pentagon has opted for the latter. It is cannibalizing missile systems across Asia-Pacific to sustain combat operations. This video shows six THAD launchers being removed from the US base in South Korea and being redeployed to the Middle East. Markets, however, don't care about battlefield victories. They're concerned with stability. If investors believe a conflict might escalate into a prolonged crisis, they begin preparing for the economic consequences long before those consequences fully appear. Data centers shut down. Shipping companies change routes, capital starts moving towards safer assets and so on. The closing of the straight of Hormuz, for instance, doesn't just affect fuel prices. It ripples through freight, food, housing, and even water infrastructure. Modern life rests on stable energy flows. And once those begin to fluctuate, the effects spread outward. So while military planners focus on operational objectives, political leaders must also consider how the conflict is upsetting inflation, energy prices, and the broader economy. Even superpowers must negotiate with reality. We may be living in what feels like the most anxietyinducing era in recent memory. Not necessarily the most dangerous period in history, but one that often feels that way. Between alarming headlines, endless commentary, and the temptation to keep doom scrolling, it's easy to feel overwhelmed by everything happening around us. I caught myself in that spiral recently, just scrolling through updates late at night, one headline after another. At some point, you're no longer staying informed. You're just feeding the anxiety. One thing that can help is simply having space to step back and process it all. For many people, therapy provides that space, a chance to reflect, gain perspective, and better understand the patterns shaping how we think and respond to stress. BetterHelp, the sponsor of today's episode, makes it easier to start therapy. You can take a short quiz and get matched with a credentialed therapist and you can communicate in the way that works best for you, whether by phone, video, or text. And if the match isn't right, you can switch therapists at any time at no extra cost. More than 6 million people have already gotten help through BetterHelp. If you're interested, click the link in the description or go to betterhelp.com/caspianreport to get 10% off your first month of therapy. The first pressure point in modern warfare is munitions. Everything hinges on this. At first glance, the US military appears almost limitless in firepower. Precision missiles can strike targets hundreds of kilometers away. Satellites track movements in real time, while air defense systems intercept rockets mid-flight. It almost looks as if advanced militaries can simply keep fighting for as long as they want. But there is a quiet reality behind all of this. Modern weapons are extraordinarily difficult to produce. A Tomahawk missile is not just a metal tube filled with explosives. It contains specialized electronics, advanced guidance systems, and components that come from long supply chains. Many of those parts are produced in small quantities by only a handful of manufacturers. The same is true for interceptor missiles, long range drones, and precisiong guided bombs, which means these weapons cannot be replaced quickly. At the start of a conflict, this problem is easy to miss. Militaries rely on stockpiles built up over years. Those reserves allow them to sustain a high tempo of strikes in the early stages of a war. Missiles fly, air defenses intercept, and so commanders operate as if supply is not an issue. But stockpiles don't last forever, and once they begin to shrink, the war starts to run into industrial constraints. Factories cannot scale production overnight. Doing so would require time, skilled labor, and above all, multi-year contracts with suppliers. Take the SM3 interceptor missile as an example. The US Navy uses it to shoot down ballistic missiles. Depending on the variant, each missile costs roughly 10 to 28 million. That price tag reflects its complexity. The missile must detect a ballistic warhead in space, track it, and collide with it at several kilometers/s using a kinetic kill vehicle. It's essentially a small spacecraft designed to destroy another object traveling faster than a bullet. But because of that complexity, the production of SM3 missiles is limited. The exact number is classified, but they're produced in relatively small batches. often only dozens per year depending on the Pentagon's procurements. Another example is the Patriot Pack 3 Interceptor, one of the main missiles used by America and Israel to shoot down Iranian missiles. Each Pac 3 interceptor costs roughly 4 to 5 million. However, in spite of its widespread use, production is relatively limited. In 2025, manufacturer Loheed Martin produced around 620 PAC 3 interceptors. That seems plenty at first, but modern air defense systems often fire multiple interceptors at a single incoming missile to ensure a successful kill. In a prolonged highintensity conflict, this equation gradually shifts the nature of the war. One night of missile defense can burn through months of production. This video shows over a dozen Patriot interceptors launched from the local US air base during an Iranian missile barrage. That's about 2% of the Patriots annual production gone in under a minute. No war machine runs this hot forever. The same munitions constraint exists on the Iranian side, though it looks very different. Iran possesses one of the largest ballistic missile arsenals in the Middle East, estimated at several thousand. But missiles alone do not determine how much firepower a country can bring to the battlefield. They also need launchers. These launch vehicles must constantly move, hide, and reposition. The moment a missile is fired, sensors and satellites can often trace the launch back to its origin, making the vehicle itself a prime target. Destroy enough of these launchers, and even a large missile stockpile becomes useless. Iran has also invested heavily in drones, which push the economics of war even further. Systems like the Shahed 136 are rudimentary when compared to missiles, but they're built with small engines and basic electronics and are estimated to cost between 20 and $50,000 each with some estimates going as low as 7,000. Launched in waves, these drones force defenders to spend far more expensive interceptors, gradually saturating air defenses and exhausting stockpiles faster than they can be replenished. Altogether, these dynamics show that modern warfare depends as much on industry as on tactics. Victory belongs to the side that can sustain the flow of weapons. Armed conflicts today face another pressure point that did not exist to the same degree in the past. Financial markets. The moment fighting breaks out in a strategically important region, energy prices move within hours. Transportation costs rise and investors start reassessing risks. Often times, these market fluctuations happen long before governments decide how to respond. We're already seeing this dynamic unfold. Oil prices jumped as soon as hostilities began to disrupt traffic near the straight of Hormuz. Governments moved quickly to calm markets by releasing strategic reserves and signaling that additional supplies could be brought online if needed. Those measures helped stabilize prices for the moment. But the episode illustrates how sensitive global markets are. And this is not just about oil. Once energy markets begin moving, the effects trickle down. Freight becomes more expensive, manufacturing costs rise, and inflation begins creeping upward again. All these disruptions move far faster than military campaigns, and they ripple through global supply chains. Fertilizer production, for example, depends heavily on natural gas. When energy prices rise, the cost of producing ammonia, the key ingredient in nitrogen fertilizers, rises as well. That increase eventually reaches farmers, which months from now raises the cost of staple crops such as wheat, corn, and rice. Global aviation is another example. The Middle East sits at the crossroads of major air routts connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa. About 2/3 of the global population lives within an 8-hour flight of Doha and Dubai. So when missiles, drones, or air defense systems threaten regional airspace, carriers are forced to reroute flights around the danger zones. This is how the region's airspace looks right now. Azerbaijan is effectively the single direct link between Europe and Asia. But it's more than just that. The trickle down consequences don't necessarily stay local. Distant sectors feel them too. Much of the recent momentum in the American stock market and a hefty portion of US economic growth is driven by a handful of tech giants, often referred to as the Magnificent 7. These companies dominate the market. In 2023 alone, they accounted for around 60% of the SNP500's total return, which goes to show just how concentrated the market rally has become. However, the expansion of these tech giants depends on massive investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure, particularly the data centers that power cloud computing and machine learning. The UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Bahrain have been actively courting these tech giants to host regional cloud and AI hubs in an effort to position themselves as digital infrastructure centers. But Iran treats this digital infrastructure as part of the conflict itself. Iranian drones have already damaged Amazon data centers in the UAE and Bahrain which have disrupted cloud services used by banks and companies in the region. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Nvidia, IBM, Oracle and Palanteer are now all legitimate targets according to the IRGC. By threatening or damaging the overseas infrastructure of these firms, Iran is attempting to hurt the digital backbone of the American tech sector and by extension a key engine of US economic growth. Pipelines, shipping, fertilizers, data centers. That's just the start. The ripple effects run even deeper into the global economy. Prochemical production relies heavily on oil and gas feed stocks. Semiconductor supply chains depend on predictable shipping routes and specialized industrial materials. Gulf sovereign wealth funds manage trillions of dollars in assets worldwide. So any instability that forces them to move their capital can echo across financial markets. Taken together, these examples reveal just how many critical systems underpin the global economy. A prolonged conflict with Iran will shape prices, supply chains, and growth across the planet. And as those disruptions mount, the White House will gradually yield to investors and markets. Politics is the third and final pressure point. It's less visible than weapons or markets, but just as powerful. While military campaigns can stretch for years, elections arrive on schedule. And that mismatch eventually creates pressure. At the start of a conflict, political leaders usually enjoy broad public support. Governments have room to act and military operations move forward with relatively little domestic resistance. But that unity rarely lasts forever. As hostilities drag on, questions begin to surface. What are the objectives? How long will this continue? What are the costs? Those questions grow louder once the war begins to affect everyday life, whether through rising fuel costs, higher inflation, or the steady drip of casualties. In the United States, the next political clock is always ticking. Every 2 years, Americans elect a new Congress. The next one is scheduled for November 2026. In that election, all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and roughly onethird of the seats in the Senate will be on the ballot. These midterm elections often become a referendum on the sitting president's policies, especially during periods of economic stress or military conflict. A war that drags on too long, can quickly turn into a political liability, even if the fighting itself remains far away. Lawmakers, particularly those from swing districts and swing states, are usually the first to distance themselves from unpopular policies. Not necessarily because the war has been lost, but because the domestic political environment can no longer sustain it. For a president, that creates a dilemma. Armies can fight for as long as their supplies last. Economies can absorb shocks for a time. But political legitimacy must be renewed at the ballot box. So if the war with Iran drags on long enough to collide with the midterm election, the pressure will not only come from the battlefield or the markets, it will also come from Capitol Hill. When viewed together, munitions, markets, and midterms will determine the outcome of this conflict. Each of these pressure points can shape political decisions. Iran understands this dynamic and leans into it. The attacks on tankers and data centers are meant to stretch missile supply chains, unsettle global markets, and wait for political pressure in Washington to build. And as these pressure points converge at the same time, they will begin to narrow Trump's room for maneuver. Before long, total victory is spun into acceptable outcome. That would be the tradeoff. There is a sense of irony in all this. The war meant to weaken Iran could instead leave the country with Kamina just 30 years younger. I've been your host Shervan from Caspian Report. If you enjoy these videos, consider supporting the channel on Patreon and click the bell icon so the next one doesn't slip past you. Thank you for your time and s

Iran war as 1973 Arab oil crisis parallel: energy security imperative → nuclear buildout → structural uranium demand. glossary.llm_summary: The petrodollar system: in 1974, Kissinger made a deal with Saudi Arabia — sell oil only in USD, US provides military protection. Every oil-importing country (effectively everyone) must hold dollars to buy energy, creating permanent structural demand for USD regardless of US economic performance. Petrodollar recycling: Saudi/Gulf sovereign wealth reinvests oil revenues into US debt, stocks, and real estate — money flows out to buy oil then straight back in as investment. This gives the US three permanent advantages: stronger dollar than fundamentals justify, lower bond yields (everyone must hold US treasuries), and the ability to economically destroy countries via sanctions (Russia 2022 example). The system is now cracking: China/Russia/India/Saudi Arabia are trading oil in non-dollar currencies. Dollar's share of global reserves has fallen from 70% to 58%. Felix argues the petrodollar is in its 'newspaper moment' — won't collapse suddenly but will erode trade-by-trade. For ASX: dollar decline benefits AUD (commodity currency), commodity exporters, and energy transition stocks.

He rose after Ibrahim Raisi died in a helicopter crash in 2024. A three-person wartime council — moderate president Peshkan, hardline judiciary head, and senior cleric — is holding power in parallel. Senior IRGC commanders are being systematically killed by Israeli strikes, creating internal power flux. Iran doesn't need a Supreme Leader to launch missiles, but succession stability matters for post-war Iran. The IRGC remains the real kingmaker. Leadership uncertainty prolongs the conflict and sustains the geopolitical risk premium on energy.

glossary.title: How the Iran War set off a regional conflict
glossary.llm_summary: US-Israeli strikes have expanded beyond nuclear sites to decapitation strikes on Iran's political and military leadership including the Supreme Leader. Iran is retaliating asymmetrically by firing missiles at Arab oil states — Jordan, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Syria, UAE — roughly as many missiles aimed at Arab nations as at Israel. Iran's strategy: convert Gulf Arab vulnerability into American political pressure by forcing Gulf leaders (who have real influence with Trump) to lobby for de-escalation. Iran has also shut the Strait of Hormuz, stranding ~1,000 ships in the Persian Gulf and pushing Brent crude above $100. The IEA has proposed its largest ever emergency oil reserve release (400 million barrels). Iran understands it cannot win conventionally and is playing for asymmetric costs: American casualties (referencing 1983 Beirut barracks withdrawal), energy price shock, and Gulf Arab pressure on Trump. A 70% majority of Americans oppose military intervention in Iran.

glossary.title: Is Oil the Next Commodity to Rip? (Josh Young)
glossary.llm_summary:
Josh Young (Bison Interests, Houston) makes the case that oil is the next commodity cycle to run, directly paralleling the experience of mining investors who have watched copper, gold, and lithium lead first.

Supply side: US shale has been kept alive by technology (laterals extended from 1 mile to 4 miles, massively reducing per-well capex), but this is now rolling over in 2026 — drilling must grow just to stay flat due to 5-8% global decline rates. Canada is effectively landlocked (no new pipelines approved, government redirecting royalty revenue from Alberta). Brazil is near capacity at 4M bbl/day. Ghana cannot scale from 1M to 3M. New supply is genuinely unclear.

Demand side: Josh's base case is >1% demand growth per year, which no major agency (IEA, OPEC, banks) is forecasting through 2050 — despite actual recent data showing 2.1-2.4M bbl/day growth in a single year. He argues China is likely understating oil consumption and inflating storage data to buy crude $10/barrel cheaper (a strategy consistent with how Chinese counterparties behave in physical oil trades, per the traders he has spoken to).

Data quality: The oil market data is described as "abysmal" — the EIA published a figure of 24M bbl/day US liquids production which Josh calls clearly wrong (double-counting refinery output). Every major provider is "wrong all the time."

The single most important variable: "If the US bombs Iran" — identified in the opening as the factor that would matter more for oil markets than anything else over a 12-month horizon. This was recorded before the Iran war started, making it prescient.

Valuation: Oil majors (Exxon etc.) are expensive, earnings declining as stocks rise. Best value is oil field services — drilling rigs, offshore drillers, completion companies — trading at large discounts to replacement cost and cheap cash flow multiples. Josh draws explicit parallel to Australian mining services stocks. Direct ASX read-through: energy producers (WDS, STO) and oil field services exposed. Oil price above $100 is an inflation shock for RBA and ASX rate-sensitive sectors.

glossary.title: Three ways Trump could strike Iran
glossary.llm_summary: Pre-war analysis of how the US would strike Iran: the objective ranges from destroying nuclear sites (B-2 bombers with GBU-57 bunker busters, same as June 2025) to full regime change. 400kg of 60%-enriched uranium was relocated before the first strikes — enough for nine nuclear weapons if further enriched to 90% — making the war unfinished. Three attack corridors analysed: northern (over Black Sea/Caucasus, risks Russian detection), central (through Jordan/Iraq, tested and preferred, over 36 US tanker aircraft pre-positioned in Jordan), and southern (Indian Ocean via USS Abraham Lincoln, more firepower with B-52s). Regime change would require weeks of sustained strikes, not a one-off. If Iran collapses, Israeli jets stand ready to immediately demolish Iran's entire military infrastructure — same playbook as Syria post-Assad. Iran's response tiers: telegraphed limited strike (low), Gulf base attacks (mid), Strait of Hormuz closure or unannounced attack on US/Israeli targets (high/existential).
glossary.transcript_text: The Pentagon is gathering air power for a massive attack on Iran, possibly with the intent of regime change. The USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group is moving toward the Middle East. Patriot and Thad air defense systems are being deployed. Non-essential US personnel and equipment are being pulled back from exposed regional bases. and over three dozen US tanker aircraft and heavy lift transporters are heading there. The planning phase is now giving way to execution. Iran, meanwhile, is not sitting idly by. Russian and Chinese cargo aircraft have been making rounds into the country, almost certainly carrying arms and ammunition. Since mid 2025, Thran has been stockpiling arms, specifically Chinese weapons. On paper, Iran now fields top-notch air defenses, including HQ9B missiles. In practice, however, that advantage is brittle. Air defense systems only work efficiently when layered and integrated with other systems. Iran doesn't have that. For two decades, Venezuela has been the single largest driver of regional instability, fueling mass migration, crossber crime, and economic distress across the continent. With the arbitrator of that system gone, the coalition is now at risk of splintering. The decisive variable is the military. He prefers Vice President Deli Rodriguez as interim leader on the condition that she delivers on US demands. If she fails, the White House has threatened to use its naval task force in the Caribbean to cut off oil exports. Venezuela's economic lifeline. But it's not that black and white. Meeting those conditions would directly threaten the military factions that profit from them and set Rodriguez against some very powerful associates. Long-erving defense minister Vladimir Padrino and Interior Minister Diostad Cabo control most of Venezuela's hard power. Padrino runs the armed forces while Cababelloo commands the collectivos which is a collection of paramilitary forces used to intimidate rivals and snuff out descent. glossary.llm_summary: Nixon severed the dollar-gold link on August 15, 1971 — from that point governments gained the ability to create money at will and global debt took on a life of its own, growing from billions to $345 trillion today (3x global GDP). The US alone owes $38 trillion, 70% to its own citizens through the bank-pension-insurance loop (US commercial banks hold $4.6 trillion in Treasury bonds). The remaining 30% is foreign-held. The system is self-reinforcing: to repay old debt, governments borrow more; economies require constant money circulation to function; stopping overnight would collapse public spending and trigger recession (as nearly happened in COVID). The risk is perception-driven — when confidence breaks, borrowing costs spike, forcing governments to choose between spending cuts, tax hikes, or money printing (inflation). Zimbabwe 2008 is the extreme case. For ASX: structural global debt and money printing sustain inflation expectations, support commodity prices long-term, and pressure central banks including the RBA.
glossary.transcript_text: It's August 15th, 1971. President Richard Nixon appears on live television and announces that the United States will no longer convert dollars into gold. >> I have directed Secretary Connley to suspend temporarily the convertability of the dollar into gold or other reserve assets. >> It seems like a minor technicality, but what follows is monumental. Money once anchored to something physical becomes pure fiat currency backed by nothing more than government decree. Immediately thereafter things begin to change. Global debt takes a life of its own and over the next few decades it balloons from billions to trillions. Today it stands at $345 trillion give or take. That's three times the size of the entire global economy. America alone accounts for 38 trillion of that. But there's something strange about all this. You see, the US owes China roughly $770 billion. Yet, China itself is drowning in $18 trillion worth of debt. Much of it sits with Chinese banks, the same banks that also own American debt. American banks, in turn, are holding debt from China, Europe, and just about everyone else. But here's the paradox. If everyone owes money to everyone else, then who is all that money actually going to? The answer isn't what you think. Follow the money far enough, and the trail circles back to where it started. The world essentially owes money to itself, and it works so long as no one checks the math. Today's video is sponsored by Sift. Every day, we're flooded with information. There are too many headlines, too little context, and half the story is happening in languages most of us don't even see or understand. Sift takes a completely different approach. Instead of chasing headlines, you start with a topic you actually care about. SIFT then scans trusted local and global sources across countries and languages and translates and summarizes the key developments into one clear readable feed. So you're not just seeing how a story is framed, you're seeing what's actually happening, often before it reaches mainstream coverage. It's less about comparing headlines and more about following how a topic actually evolves around the world. It's loved by thousands of people and is even the number one ranking news app in several countries. Sift builds a personalized feed around whatever you want to follow. And because it pulls from local sources worldwide, you get broader coverage, real context, and clarity you won't get from just one country's media without bouncing between the apps. It also stays on top of updates with realtime coverage and notifications. And if you want the full context, [music] you can always click through and go deeper. So if you want to actually understand what's happening in the world, not just scroll past it, search SIFT and download the app for free on the App Store or Google Play. Debt is as old as civilization itself. Long before banks or paper money, debt was simply a promise. A neighbor lends you a bag of grain in spring and come harvest you pay them back maybe with a little extra as thanks. This is how societies operated for thousands of years. However, as trade expanded beyond local communities, these arrangements grew more complex. During the Renaissance, Italian banking houses created credit instruments, ways to transfer debt rather than just hold it personally. This allowed merchants to do business across continents without carrying chests of gold. The real breakthrough, however, came in 1694 when Britain faced a funding crisis under King William III. The Royal Navy desperately needed 1.2 million to finance the war with France, but the government's credit was poor and [music] direct borrowing proved impossible. So the royal court came up with an ingenious solution. Create a corporation called the Bank of England and allow investors to become shareholders. The bank would then lend the money to the government and charge 8% interest. In return, it received government bonds which could be resold to the public or to anyone willing to buy them. Suddenly, for the first time, ordinary citizens could effectively lend money to the state through a reliable agent. It was a simple scheme, but it changed everything. States could now raise massive sums without hiking taxes or draining their treasuries. The system quickly spread across Europe and became the bedrock of early capitalism. Then, during the industrial revolution, the system went into overdrive. Factories, railroads, and infrastructure required unprecedented amounts of capital, far more than any single wealthy individual could muster. The banks that had been set up pulled saving deposits and lent them to industrialists. By doing so, borrowing became not just useful, but structurally necessary for economic growth. By the 20th century, World War I and World War II pushed countries to borrow at scales never before seen, not just to fight, but to rebuild afterward. In 1944, the Breton Woods agreement made the US dollar the centerpiece of the global financial system with currencies tied to the dollar and the dollar tied to gold. But gold was limited and economies had to grow. So, as US spending accelerated during the Vietnam War and the Great Society programs, there wasn't enough gold to back the flood of dollars circulating globally, forcing Nixon to sever the link in 1971. The consequences were profound. From that point forward, governments gained the ability to create money at will. And with the old restraints gone, a new system emerged where debt could expand as long as lenders remained confident in government decrees. Steadily throughout the 1980s, nations discovered that borrowing wasn't just useful in wartime. It could fuel peacetime growth, too. And so, governments borrowed to build schools, repair roads, and pull economies out of recession. Debt stopped being a last resort and became standard operating procedure. Today, debt is how things get built, how recessions are managed, and how political promises are kept. Debt is no longer an anomaly in the system. It has become the system itself. The United States offers the clearest example of how this self-reinforcing system actually works. With $ 38 trillion in debt, no other country comes even close. Yet, roughly 70% of that debt is owed to Americans themselves. The US in essence borrows from its own citizens. You see, when someone deposits money in a bank, it doesn't just sit in a vault. Banks put that money to work trying to grow it so they can pass some interest back to depositors. They do this by lending, investing, and buying bonds. Right now, US commercial banks hold about $4.6 trillion in Treasury bonds and other government securities, which is more than the GDP of Japan or India. Bonds are particularly popular because they're one of the safest ways to earn interest. [music] And unlike stocks that swing wildly every day, a 10-year US government bond today pays a steady annual interest rate, offering reliable returns with little risk. But banks aren't alone in this. Pension funds, insurance companies, and investment firms all do the same. So essentially, private savings have become an indirect form of government borrowing. And although it sounds odd that the US borrows from itself, think of it as money moving from parts of the country where it's sitting idle to parts where it's needed. When the government pays interest on its debt, the money flows back to lenders, giving them more cash to buy more bonds and earn more interest. It's a closed loop where money cycles endlessly from lender to borrower and back again. The same loop exists between countries. About 30% of US debt is held overseas. Foreign governments and banks buy US bonds the same way American institutions do. Money flows into the US when it borrows, flows back out when it pays interest, and the cycle repeats. And it's not just America that does this. Every country borrows, and every country lends. Japanese savings are turned into loans for the Saudis. Saudi savings become loans for Brazilians. Brazilian capital flows back into US bonds. This interconnected web creates an uneasy reality. To repay debts, governments must keep borrowing more and more. That may sound reckless, and in many ways it is, but it's also the foundation of how the global economy now works. >> [music] >> Everything from economic growth to political stability depends on this endless cycle continuing. Since debt fuels growth, governments have no choice but to borrow and spend and get money circulating in the economy. By doing so, businesses earn more. Workers get paid and as a result, they spend more. It becomes a feedback loop that keeps the economy expanding. >> [music] >> In China, about a fifth of government spending is financed by borrowing. In the US, it's one in every $4. If governments stopped borrowing overnight, public spending would fall immediately. Money would stop flowing into the economy, businesses would earn less, layoffs would increase, and [music] consumer spending would grind to a stop. That's precisely what happened when COVID hit in 2020. As people stopped spending and the economy shut down, governments stepped in and covered expenses people were unwilling to pay. In America, the government borrowed $3.1 trillion in a single year, which was about 12% of the economy at the time. China, Europe, and every other major economy did the same. It wasn't a choice [music] really. It was necessity. However, borrowed money must eventually be returned. If a government already spends everything it collects to keep the economy going, then it must take out new loans to repay the old ones. So, the debt never truly leaves the system. It just adds up. Wealthier countries such as Germany and Switzerland can afford to cycle through this system. Their bonds are considered safe, so they keep borrowing at low interest rates. But for developing nations, it's different. Higher borrowing costs make each rollover more expensive. Over time, debt starts to feed on itself. Countries like Kenya and Pakistan, for instance, are stuck in debt traps and forced to keep borrowing just to meet interest payments on past loans. So, the same debt that strengthens some economies can end up holding others back. >> [music] >> Debt-driven economies carry inherent dangers. No matter how smooth the cycle seems, risks are building beneath the surface. As governments continue borrowing, debt grows and so do interest payments. Over time, a bigger slice of the budget goes toward paying off old loans rather than funding schools, hospitals, or infrastructure. A debt to GDP ratio of about 100% is now considered normal. And frankly, debt is not a problem so long as borrowing is cheap and lenders are confident. But when political risks change and investors stop wanting to lend, borrowing costs shoot up. So perception is the real driver of the economy. One way governments keep a lid on things is by printing more money. Banks call it quantitative easing. The problem, however, is that when more money enters circulation, the value of each unit declines. The result is inflation and higher everyday costs. In extreme cases, it spirals out of control. In Zimbabwe in 2008, the government printed so much money to cover debts that prices doubled every single day. A loaf of bread that cost 10 million Zimbabwe dollars in March suddenly cost hundreds of millions by midyear and billions by November. The government eventually printed $100 trillion notes to cope with the situation, but that only made it worse. The currency became worthless and ordinary people saw their life savings vanish overnight. While most countries don't face such extremes, even moderate inflation can hurt. The risks are even bigger for developing countries which often borrow in foreign currencies such as US dollars. Meaning when their own currency weakens, debt repayments suddenly become more expensive in local terms. And as that burden grows, lenders start doubting the country's ability to repay. That's pretty much what happened in Turkey. Once the mood shifts and doubt sets in, investors tend to demand higher interest rates to compensate for the risks. And when borrowing hits a wall, governments are forced into ugly tradeoffs. They can either cut spending, raise taxes, or expand the money supply. Each of these options comes with severe consequences. All in all, the global economy is wired for constant momentum. Debt isn't a flaw. It's what keeps nations running, borrowing, lending, spending, and starting over. This perpetual motion, however, can't keep going forever. Eventually, there will be a reckoning, an economic depression. Centuries ago, physics proved that perpetual motion is impossible. Economics is yet to come around. Before we wrap up, a quick shout out to Search Party. They produce sharp, well-ressearched videos on global affairs. And if you enjoy this channel, you'll get value there, too. The link is below. I've been your host, Shivan from Caspian Report. If you approve of what we do, please leave a comment, hit the like button, and mayhaps share the video. In any case, thank you for your time and So [music] [music]
